rv.q: Mr. Guare's play is a masterpiece of American comedy, and this production does it justice.
Guare’s iconic play not only holds up, it still sets the bar for smart comic lunacy.
John Guare's 1971 comedy 'The House of Blue Leaves' receives a crackling revival that finds the perfect pitch between pathos and hilarity.

In the midst of the galloping nuns, bomb plots, shouting, love triangles and general craziness, Bananas Shaughnessy, played by a brilliant Edie Falco, emerges as the most poignant, most grounded character in a cracked universe.
John Guare saw it first and said it better.
Yet together they somehow harmonize, ably conveying Guare's gentle, genial take on the pathos of unremarkable, everyday lives.
That the play's originality still ultimately wins out is a testament to its acute observation of our perverse relationship with fame.
Together, these characters make up Broadway's most oddball gallery, flailing in a hot mess of a play.
The result is an overly dour production that gets Guare’s bitter ironies but none of his naughtiness or joy.

rv.q: This latest remount feels strangely hunkered down in itself, even as geysers of absurdity erupt willy-nilly.

As directed by David Cromer - and enacted by a talent-stuffed cast that includes Ben Stiller, Jennifer Jason Leigh and the remarkable Edie Falco - this production zooms in on every gritty grain of pain to be found in Guare's breakthrough work from 1966. Within the dimness, there is one luminous force.
Too often, his three leads seem to be in three completely different shows.
John Guare's play, which opened in a strong revival Monday at the Theatre, could have been written yesterday.

As played with anger and seething resentment by Stiller, Artie’s raspy cabaret act (delivered, in part, with Stiller’s back to the audience) is about as much fun as happy hour in the Holiday Inn in Hades.
The tone is wrong -- distancing, unpleasant, not funny enough.
Although I didn't care much for this pastiche, I was taken by the production, which unspools on a wonderfully abysmal apartment set by Scott Pask.
Shockingly, Stiller conveys none of them, leaving a hole at the center of this unbalanced House of Blue Leaves.
Although Guare's play remains quite funny, Cromer downplays most of its humor to ill effect.
Cromer leans too far toward the latter and misses the laughs.
Ben Stiller has given Artie a new sense of desperation, Edie Falco has toned Bananas down to a human level, and Jennifer Jason Leigh brings new laughs to Bunny’s weird world.
Neither Falco nor Stiller tip the balance, and the production they are in is thoroughly competent, neither uncontrollably uproarious nor unbearably upsetting.
But this overly muted rendition, while occasionally displaying moments of stunning theatricality, provides little of the sugar that would help its medicine go down.

Newcomers to “The House of Blue Leaves” are unlikely to see beyond Cromer’s misguided staging to appreciate the play itself while people who know and love it are advised to skip this unworthy occasion.
